warmup.q:
A printer writes one line per job into a log. What does firstJammed(listOf("DONE job_1", "JAMMED job_2", "DONE job_3")) return?

fun firstJammed(log: List<String>): String? {
    log.forEach { if (it.startsWith("JAMMED")) return it }
    return null
}
options: null, because return only leaves the lambda and forEach carries on
It doesn't compile: return is not allowed inside a lambda
It throws, because forEach can't be stopped early
warmup.why: forEach is an inline function, so its lambda is pasted into firstJammed, and a bare return there returns from firstJammed itself. That's a non-local return, and the section on it takes it line by line. In Java, return inside a forEach lambda would only leave the lambda, which is why the first option is tempting. Inside a lambda passed to an ordinary function, the third option would be right.

opening:
Picture a small print shop. Behind the counter sits a binder of procedure sheets: how to time a job, what to do when a printer jams. When a clerk takes a job, she can pass it to a colleague who knows the sheet, with a slip for the one step only she can do. Or she can photocopy the sheet into the job's own folder and do every step herself. The copy is quicker. It costs paper, though, and it never hears about corrections to the master.

Kotlin gives your functions the same choice, and inline is the photocopy. The surprise is that it changes what your code means, not only how fast it runs: a return inside a copied step can leave the whole job. Java habits walk straight into that.

The last track ended with Project Valhalla, which lets the JVM drop an object's identity. This track starts by dropping a whole object, the one behind a lambda. We'll watch the compiler make the copy, follow a return that leaves more than you expect, meet two modifiers for lambdas that can't be copied, and count the cost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started in a print shop that photocopies a procedure into each job's folder instead of handing it over with a slip. inline is that copy: no lambda object, no call through an interface, and a return that ends the whole job. noinline keeps a slip for the notice board, crossinline seals the night-shift envelope, and every copy stays frozen until its caller is rebuilt.

Now search your Kotlin code for a bare return inside forEach {. Each one leaves the whole function, not just the item.

Next, we'll let the compiler erase a different object: the wrapper class that gives a number its own type. When does a value class stay a plain long, and when does the box come back?

sections.h: What inline does: the compiler pastes the function and its lambda into the caller
sections.html:
Start with a helper the print shop's app uses all over the place. It runs one step of a job, such as working out how much ink the job needs, and prints how long the step took. The shop's rule of thumb is 3 ml of ink for every 100 pages:

Java
static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    try {
        return block.get();
    } finally {
        System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us");
    }
}

long ink = timed("ink", () -> pages * 3 / 100);
Kotlin
fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    try {
        return block()
    } finally {
        println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us")
    }
}

val ink = timedNotInline("ink") { pages * 3 / 100 }

The part in braces, { pages * 3 / 100 }, is a lambda: a small function written in place and passed as a value. Count what one call costs.

This lambda uses pages, a variable from outside its braces, so it is a closure: a lambda that carries the outside values it needs. To make that work, the JVM builds a small object that holds a copy of pages, and timedNotInline calls that object's invoke method. Kotlin creates the object with invokedynamic, the bytecode instruction Java also uses for its lambdas. (Bytecode is the list of instructions in a .class file that the JVM runs. The lesson "invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile", later in the course, takes that instruction apart.)

The helper is also generic: it works for any result type T. So the Long result travels back as a plain Object and has to be unboxed, that is, turned from a java.lang.Long object back into a primitive long. That's one object, one call through an interface (a type that only names its methods, here invoke) and one unboxing, on every call. The Kotlin docs name the same three costs.

In the print shop, this is the clerk handing the job to a colleague. The lambda is the slip with her own step on it, and invoke is the colleague calling her back to do it.

You could skip all of that by hand, by pasting the helper's body into the caller:

Java
long start = System.nanoTime();
long ink;
try {
    ink = pages * 3 / 100;                // the lambda's body, pasted in
} finally {
    System.out.println("ink took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us");
}
Kotlin
val start = System.nanoTime()
val ink = try {
    pages * 3 / 100                       // the lambda's body, pasted in
} finally {
    println("ink took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us")
}

Nobody writes that fifty times. The compiler, on the other hand, is happy to. Write inline fun <T> timed(...) with the same body, and the compiler stops making the call. At every call site, each place in the code that calls the function, it copies the function's body and the body of the lambda you passed. That's the photocopy: the whole procedure lands in the job's own folder, with the clerk's step written in place.

javap, a tool that comes with the JDK and prints the bytecode in a class file, shows the difference in the demo below. The ordinary call site in inkNotInline is seven instructions long. invokedynamic builds a Function0 (Kotlin's interface for a function with no parameters), invokestatic calls timedNotInline with it, and checkcast java/lang/Number plus longValue unbox the result. The inline call site has none of that. The multiply (lmul) and the divide (ldiv) sit right inside inkInline, between two calls to System.nanoTime, just like the hand-pasted version.

Read a little further and you see the price. The finally block appears twice in inkInline, once for the normal exit and once for the exit by exception. Every caller carries its own copy, so the code grows, and the docs say inlining pays off only if you avoid inlining large functions.

inline is for small functions that take lambdas.

The standard library is full of them: forEach, map, filter, let, apply, use, repeat and require are all inline. That's why jobs.map { it.pages } costs about what a hand-written loop costs. The generics track met inline for one more reason: a reified type parameter works only because the body is copied to a call site where the real type is known.

Java is where the picture breaks. A Java caller can't photocopy anything, because javac can't inline Kotlin code. For Java, InlineDemoKt.timed(...) is an ordinary static method that takes a Function0, and the Java lambda becomes an object like any other. Java always hands over the slip.

The copy changes more than speed, though. Once the clerk's step sits in her own folder, an instruction like "stop here" means something new.

steps: Run InlineDemo (or InlineDemoJava) with the command below. Both print ink = 360 ml twice.
From labs/, run javap -c -p kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemoKt.class.

code.title: InlineDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. */ inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The same function without inline: the caller builds a Function0 object and calls through it. */ fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The shop's rule of thumb: 3 ml of ink for every 100 pages. */ fun inkInline(pages: Long): Long = timed("inline") { pages * 3 / 100 } fun inkNotInline(pages: Long): Long = timedNotInline("not inline") { pages * 3 / 100 } fun main() { println("ink = ${inkInline(12_000)} ml") println("ink = ${inkNotInline(12_000)} ml") }

alt.title: InlineDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of InlineDemo.kt. javac cannot inline Kotlin code, so for Java the inline function * timed() is an ordinary static method on InlineDemoKt that takes a Function0. */ public class InlineDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // the Java lambda becomes a Function0 object; timed() calls its invoke() like any other method long ink = InlineDemoKt.timed("from Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("ink = " + ink + " ml"); // the same idea written in plain Java: a Supplier and a call through it long same = timedJava("plain Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("ink = " + same + " ml"); } static <T> T timedJava(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } }

try.expect: inkNotInline is short: invokedynamic (a new Function0), invokestatic timedNotInline, then checkcast java/lang/Number and longValue to unbox the result. inkInline holds the arithmetic (lmul, ldiv) and two PrintStream.println calls, because the finally block was copied for both exits. Ignore the microsecond timings: one cold call measures class loading and lambda setup, not inlining. The bytecode is the evidence.

sections.h: Non-local returns: a return in an inlined lambda leaves the whole function
sections.html:
Inside an ordinary lambda, a bare return doesn't compile. The error is 'return' is prohibited here. An ordinary lambda is an object with its own invoke method, and code inside that method has no way to make some other function return. An inlined lambda is different. Its body becomes part of the caller, so return can mean exactly what it says.

The print shop's printers write one line per job into a log, such as DONE job_1 or JAMMED job_2 in tray 2. Here are two small functions that read such a log:

Java
static String firstJammed(List<String> log) {
    for (String line : log) {
        if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return line;  // Java needs a real loop to return early
    }
    return null;
}

static int countDone(List<String> log) {
    int done = 0;
    for (String line : log) {
        if (!line.startsWith("DONE")) continue;
        done++;
    }
    return done;
}
Kotlin
fun firstJammed(log: List<String>): String? {
    log.forEach { if (it.startsWith("JAMMED")) return it }   // leaves firstJammed
    return null
}

fun countDone(log: List<String>): Int {
    var done = 0
    log.forEach {
        if (!it.startsWith("DONE")) return@forEach           // leaves this lambda call only
        done++
    }
    return done
}

The first return is a non-local return: it leaves the function that contains the lambda, firstJammed, not only the lambda. It compiles only because forEach is inline. In the bytecode, firstJammed is a plain loop over an Iterator, with an areturn (the instruction that returns an object) in the middle, and no lambda object exists at all.

That's the photocopy at work. The clerk's step is now written in her own folder, so when it says "stop here", she stops the whole job, not just her step. There's no colleague left to stop.

To leave only the current call of the lambda, add a label. return@forEach means "return from this call of the lambda passed to forEach", and it behaves like continue in a loop, as in countDone.

Since Kotlin 2.2.0, break and continue also work inside a lambda passed to an inline function. The feature is stable, so you need no compiler flag. The demo's pagesUntilEmpty adds up the pages of several batches of jobs, where -1 means the paper ran out. Its break inside batch.forEach { } leaves the outer for loop, the way Java's labeled break outer does.

Java has no non-local return. A Java lambda always compiles to a separate method, so return inside forEach(line -> { ... }) only ends that one call, and the loop goes on. The Java twin's firstJammedBroken shows it: it always returns null.

That difference sets a trap for anyone who learned Java first. In Java, return inside a forEach lambda skips to the next item, and the habit travels:

Java
jobs.forEach(job -> {
    if (job.pages() == 0) return;          // Java: skips this job, carries on
    printer.print(job);
});
Kotlin
jobs.forEach { job ->
    if (job.pages == 0) return             // Kotlin: leaves the whole function
    printer.print(job)
}

The Kotlin version compiles without a warning. The first job with no pages ends the whole function, and every job after it is silently left unprinted. The function simply goes home early. Write return@forEach to skip one item, or use a plain for loop with continue, which reads better anyway.

In an inlined lambda, a bare return leaves the whole function. To skip one item, write return@forEach.

All of this works because the lambda's body is pasted into the caller's own code. Some functions can't allow that, because they keep the lambda for later or hand it to someone else.

steps: Run NonLocalReturnDemo and then NonLocalReturnDemoJava. Before you run the Java one, predict what firstJammedBroken prints.
Work out pagesUntilEmpty by hand from the three batches in main, then check your number against the output.
Uncomment the wrong move at the bottom of main (a lambda stored in a val). Predict the error, run, then comment it out again.

code.title: NonLocalReturnDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** A bare `return` inside forEach's lambda returns from firstJammed: forEach is inline. */ fun firstJammed(log: List<String>): String? { log.forEach { if (it.startsWith("JAMMED")) return it } return null } /** `return@forEach` leaves only the current lambda call, like `continue` in a loop. */ fun countDone(log: List<String>): Int { var done = 0 log.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("DONE")) return@forEach done++ } return done } /** Since Kotlin 2.2, `break` and `continue` work inside an inlined lambda too. */ fun pagesUntilEmpty(batches: List<List<Long>>): Long { var total = 0L for (batch in batches) { batch.forEach { pages -> if (pages < 0) break // -1 means "out of paper": leaves the for loop, not just the lambda total += pages } } return total } fun main() { val log = listOf("DONE job_1", "JAMMED job_2 in tray 2", "DONE job_3") println("firstJammed = ${firstJammed(log)}") println("countDone = ${countDone(log)}") println("pagesUntilEmpty = ${pagesUntilEmpty(listOf(listOf(1_000L, 250L), listOf(400L, -1L, 900L), listOf(75L)))}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val lookup = { line: String -> if (line.isEmpty()) return; line.length } }

alt.title: NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of NonLocalReturnDemo.kt. A Java lambda is always a separate method, so `return` * inside it only leaves the lambda. To return from the enclosing method you need a real loop. */ public class NonLocalReturnDemoJava { static String firstJammed(List<String> log) { for (String line : log) { if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return line; // a loop, so return leaves the method } return null; } static String firstJammedBroken(List<String> log) { log.forEach(line -> { if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return; // leaves this lambda call only }); return null; // always reached } static long pagesUntilEmpty(List<List<Long>> batches) { long total = 0; outer: for (List<Long> batch : batches) { for (long pages : batch) { if (pages < 0) break outer; // Java's labeled break: Kotlin's non-local break total += pages; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = List.of("DONE job_1", "JAMMED job_2 in tray 2", "DONE job_3"); System.out.println("firstJammed = " + firstJammed(log)); System.out.println("firstJammedBroken = " + firstJammedBroken(log)); System.out.println("pagesUntilEmpty = " + pagesUntilEmpty(List.of(List.of(1_000L, 250L), List.of(400L, -1L, 900L), List.of(75L)))); } }

Java's firstJammedBroken prints null. The wrong move fails with 'return' is prohibited here.: a lambda stored in a val is an object, so it can't return from main.

sections.h: When a lambda can't be copied: noinline and crossinline
sections.html:
Inlining works only if the compiler can paste the lambda's body where you call it. Two things get in the way, and each one has its own modifier.

The first is using the lambda as a value. An inlined lambda has no object behind it, so you can't store it in a field, add it to a list or pass it to an ordinary function. Try it, and the compiler says illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Add 'noinline' modifier to the parameter declaration. noinline turns that one parameter back into a normal lambda object. The function's other lambda parameters are still inlined.

In the print shop, that's a note that has to stay a separate slip, because it gets pinned to the notice board. A photocopy inside one folder would be no use to whoever reads the board later.

The second is calling the lambda from somewhere else: from inside an object, a Runnable or another lambda. The docs call this "another execution context". That code may run later, on another thread (a separate path of execution inside the same program), when the caller may have returned long ago. A non-local return from there can't work, so the compiler stops you: cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'task: () -> Unit'.

In the print shop, it's a set of steps sealed in an envelope for the night shift. Nobody may write "stop the whole job" inside, because by the time the night shift opens the envelope, the clerk has gone home.

crossinline is that rule, applied to the caller's lambda: no bare return inside it. With the rule in place, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Runnable class it generates for that call site. In the demo, javap finds a class called ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 with no Function0 field: the body of main's lambda sits inside its run().

Here is the pair. An executor is a JDK object that runs tasks on threads it manages; nightShift has one thread, named night-shift:

Java
// Java lambdas already behave like crossinline ones: return leaves only the lambda
static void runInBackground(Executor executor, Runnable task) {
    executor.execute(task);
}

runInBackground(nightShift, () -> System.out.println("printing tomorrow's flyers"));
Kotlin
inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) {
    executor.execute { task() }            // task runs later, on the executor's thread
}

runInBackground(nightShift) { println("printing tomorrow's flyers") }
// runInBackground(nightShift) { return }  // error: 'return' is prohibited here.

Here the picture breaks a little. A real night-shift worker who reads "stop the whole job" can shrug and ignore it. The compiler can't shrug, so it refuses to seal the envelope until the lambda promises not to leave early.

Both modifiers would make runInBackground compile, so choose by what you do with the lambda. Use crossinline when you call it inside another lambda or object, because its body is still inlined into the new class. Use noinline when the lambda has to exist as a value you keep or hand on. Neither modifier changes the JVM signature: Java sees a Function0 either way.

Keep the lambda: noinline. Let someone else call it later: crossinline.

You'll need crossinline more often than you might think. Plenty of Java APIs take a callback to run later: Executor.execute(Runnable), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier), new Thread(Runnable). Every inline Kotlin wrapper around one of them needs it.

So far inline looks like a free upgrade with two small rules. It isn't free, and the next section adds up the bill.

try.title: Make the compiler ask for each modifier
steps: Run ModifiersDemo (or ModifiersDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions with plain Java lambdas).
In ModifiersDemo.kt, delete noinline in subscribe. Predict the error, run, read it, then put it back.
Delete crossinline in runInBackground, run, and put it back.
Uncomment the last line of main and run. Why does the compiler refuse a return that it allowed in forEach?

code.title: ModifiersDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.Executor import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() /** noinline: `listener` is stored in a list, so it has to stay a real object. `log` is inlined. */ inline fun subscribe(log: (String) -> Unit, noinline listener: (String) -> Unit) { log("subscribing listener #${listeners.size + 1}") listeners += listener } /** crossinline: `task` runs inside a Runnable on another thread, so it may not return from the caller. */ inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } } fun main() { subscribe({ println(it) }) { event -> println("listener got $event") } listeners.forEach { it("job-finished") } val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "night-shift") } runInBackground(pool) { println("running on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, then undo. // 1. Delete `noinline` in subscribe. // 2. Delete `crossinline` in runInBackground. // 3. Uncomment the next line. // runInBackground(pool) { return } }

alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Java twin of ModifiersDemo.kt. noinline and crossinline leave no trace in the method signature: * Java sees plain Function0 and Function1 parameters. Every Java lambda already behaves like a * crossinline one, because `return` in a Java lambda can only leave the lambda. */ public class ModifiersDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { // subscribe(Function1<? super String, Unit>, Function1<? super String, Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.subscribe( line -> { System.out.println(line); return Unit.INSTANCE; }, event -> { System.out.println("listener got " + event); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); ModifiersDemoKt.getListeners().forEach(l -> l.invoke("job-finished")); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "night-shift")); // runInBackground(Executor, Function0<Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.runInBackground(pool, () -> { System.out.println("running on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: The first run prints subscribing listener #1, listener got job-finished and running on night-shift. Without noinline the build fails with illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Without crossinline it fails with cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. The last line fails with 'return' is prohibited here.: by the time the Runnable runs on the night-shift thread, main may be somewhere else entirely. once compiles without crossinline: run is inline too, so block is still pasted into the caller's own code, and a return in it still has a function to leave. Swap run for an ordinary function that takes a lambda and the error comes back.

sections.h: When not to inline: code size, frozen copies and visibility
sections.html:
inline has three costs, and all three show up in real code.

The first is size. The body is copied into every caller, so a 40-line function called from 200 places becomes 200 copies, and every folder in the shop gets thicker. The compiler even warns when you inline a function that takes no lambdas: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. Inlining works best for functions with parameters of function types. Without a lambda there is nothing to remove: no object, no call through an interface. And the JIT, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while the program runs, already inlines small, hot methods by itself.

The second is frozen copies. A caller gets its copy of the body when the caller is compiled. In one test, a small app was compiled against version 1 of a library. Then version 2 replaced the library's jar (the zip file a library ships in) without recompiling the app. The app printed inline=v1 plain=v2. The ordinary function ran the new code, and the inline one still ran its old copy. It's the photocopy that never heard about the correction.

So if you publish a library that other programs use, treat a public inline body like a public signature. A fix inside it reaches each program only when that program is rebuilt.

The third is visibility, and it follows from the second. The body lands in other modules, the separately compiled parts of a program, such as a library and the app that uses it. So it may only use what those modules can use. Call a private function from a public inline one, and you get public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function.

The fix is @PublishedApi internal. internal means visible only inside this module, and @PublishedApi makes the function public in the bytecode anyway, so the pasted copies can reach it. The helper's own body isn't copied anywhere, so it can use private state freely. Here it hands out trace ids, labels that tie the start and end lines of one operation together in the log:

Java
// Java has no internal or inline. The nearest shape: one public helper that callers reach
public final class Tracing {
    private static final AtomicInteger COUNTER = new AtomicInteger();
    public static String nextTraceId() { return "trace-" + COUNTER.incrementAndGet(); }
}
Kotlin
inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T {
    val id = nextTraceId()                  // must be reachable from every caller's module
    println("[$id] start $operation")
    val result = block()
    println("[$id] end $operation")
    return result
}

@PublishedApi
internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet()

private val counter = AtomicInteger()       // fine: nextTraceId is not inline

The compiler adds two hard limits. An inline function can't call itself (inline function 'fun recI(n: Int): Int' cannot be recursive.), and it can't contain a local function (local functions are not yet supported in inline functions.).

Properties can be inline too, as long as the accessor has no backing field, that is, no stored value of its own. The demo's val Long.asKilos: String inline get() = ... turns 1,999 grams into 1.999 kg. You'll mostly see inline properties when they need a reified type parameter.

My rule: inline small functions that take lambdas, or that need reified or a non-local return, and leave everything else ordinary. When an inline body starts to grow, split it.

Keep the inline part to a few lines, and move the real work into a @PublishedApi internal function that is compiled once.

The lab puts all of this into one small helper: a retry for a printer that sometimes jams, with a non-local return, a crossinline lambda and a @PublishedApi door.

try.title: Break the visibility rule
steps: Run PublishedApiDemo, then PublishedApiDemoJava.
In PublishedApiDemo.kt, change @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId() to private fun nextTraceId(). Predict the error and run the Kotlin demo.
Put it back. Why can the Java twin call nextTraceId() directly, when Kotlin code in another module could not?

code.title: PublishedApiDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * A public inline function is pasted into callers, possibly in another module. So its body may * only use declarations those callers could use themselves. */ inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } /** Not part of the Kotlin API, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can call it. */ @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline, so its body is never copied /** An inline property: no backing field, and the getter is pasted into each caller. */ val Long.asKilos: String inline get() = "" + (this / 1_000) + "." + (this % 1_000).toString().padStart(3, '0') + " kg" fun main() { val grams = traced("weigh parcel job_7") { 1_999L } println("parcel weighs ${grams.asKilos}") // Wrong move. Change `@PublishedApi internal` on nextTraceId to `private`, predict, run. }

alt.title: PublishedApiDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of PublishedApiDemo.kt. `internal` is a Kotlin rule that javac does not know about. * In the bytecode nextTraceId() is public, so Java can call it, and traced() is an ordinary method. */ public class PublishedApiDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { long grams = PublishedApiDemoKt.traced("weigh parcel job_7", () -> 1_999L); System.out.println("parcel weighs " + PublishedApiDemoKt.getAsKilos(grams)); System.out.println("Java can call the internal helper too: " + PublishedApiDemoKt.nextTraceId()); } }

try.expect: Both print [trace-1] start weigh parcel job_7, [trace-1] end weigh parcel job_7 and parcel weighs 1.999 kg, and the Java twin also prints trace-2 from a direct call. With private, the build fails with public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. internal is a Kotlin rule. In the bytecode the function is public, and javac doesn't know the rule exists.

aside.title: Doesn't the JIT inline everything anyway?
aside.html: It inlines a lot, but it's a different tool. The JIT inlines while the program runs, only on hot paths, and it can undo its choice when its guesses turn out wrong. Kotlin inlines at compile time, at every call site, before the JVM ever sees the code. Only the compile-time kind can change what the code means, which is why a non-local return and a reified type need it. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers the JIT's side.

compare.title: Wrapping a callback API: Java Supplier vs Kotlin inline with crossinline

java.title: Timing.java
java.html: import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Timing { static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // the caller's lambda is an object; supplyAsync gets a second lambda that calls it static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); } } // call site: Timing.timedAsync("print", nightShift, () -> printer.print(job));

kotlin.title: Timing.kt
kotlin.html: import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executor inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block runs inside the Supplier, another execution context: crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor) // call site: timedAsync("print", nightShift) { printer.print(job) }

compare.note: Both versions time a step on another thread and hand back a future, a placeholder for a result that arrives later. In Java the caller's lambda is always an object, and timedAsync wraps it in a second one for supplyAsync. In Kotlin the compiler pastes both timed and the caller's lambda into one Supplier class that it generates for that call site, so there is one object instead of two, and no call through Supplier.get on the caller's code. The bigger difference is the rule for the caller: inside the Kotlin block, a bare return is a compile error, while a Java lambda simply can't express one. Java code that calls the Kotlin timedAsync gets the ordinary compiled body and passes a Function0.

worked.title: Write an inline helper over a Java callback API

steps.say: A Java library (invented for this example) lets one job at a time use the shop's printer. You pass the work as a Callable, the JDK's interface for a task that returns a value, and the library runs it while it holds the printer, so two jobs never mix their pages. You want Kotlin callers to write queue.printing { printer.print(job) }. Start with the API and an ordinary Kotlin wrapper.
steps.code: public interface PrinterQueue { <T> T withPrinter(Callable<T> work); } // Java callers write the Callable themselves int pages = queue.withPrinter(() -> printer.print(flyers));

alt.html: interface PrinterQueue { fun <T> withPrinter(work: Callable<T>): T } // 1. an ordinary wrapper: it works, but each call builds a Function0 and a Callable fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() })

steps.say: The wrapper is one line and runs for every job, so make it inline. The compiler refuses, because block() is now called inside the Callable, which the library may run later or on another thread.
steps.code: // 2. add inline: the compiler stops here inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() }) // error: cannot inline 'block: () -> T' here: it might contain non-local returns. // Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block: () -> T'.

alt.html: // Java has no inline and no non-local return, so the question never comes up: // a return inside the Callable lambda only ends the Callable int pages = queue.withPrinter(() -> { printer.print(flyers); return flyers.pages(); });

steps.say: Add crossinline. The caller's lambda is now pasted into a Callable class that the compiler generates for each call site. In exchange, callers lose the non-local return: that's the rule crossinline enforces.
steps.code: // 3. crossinline: inlined into the generated Callable, no bare return allowed inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(crossinline block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() }) fun send(job: Job) { queue.printing { printer.print(job) } // queue.printing { if (job.isEmpty) return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. }

alt.html: void send(Job job) { queue.withPrinter(() -> { printer.print(job); return null; // Callable must return something }); }

steps.say: Check that it earns its place. It does: one line, a lambda parameter, called for every job. If it later grows logging, timing and error handling, keep the inline part to this one line and move the rest into a @PublishedApi internal function, so 300 call sites don't each carry a copy.

lab.title: An inline retry helper, sync and async
steps: A printer that jams on the first try often works on the second, so the shop's app retries. Run the tests. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. Read Callers.kt but don't edit it: the tests go through it, and its comment says why.
Write retry (TODO 1). Start at attempt 1, return block(attempt) inside a try, catch Exception, and decide whether to go round again. Keep the earlier failures in a list.
When you stop, throw giveUp(attempt, e, earlier). The build now fails. Read the error, and fix the declaration of giveUp (TODO 2), not retry.
Write retryAsync (TODO 3) as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ retry(maxAttempts) { block(it) } }, executor). Add the modifier the compiler asks for.
Run the tests until all eight pass, including RetryFromJavaTest, which calls your retry from Java with no inlining at all.
Optional: add crossinline to retry's block and run again. Callers.firstAccepted stops compiling, because its return printer is a non-local return. Undo it.
hints: require(maxAttempts >= 1) { "maxAttempts must be at least 1" } throws IllegalArgumentException before the loop starts, so the block is never called.
A while (true) loop whose body ends only with return or throw needs no return after it. The compiler knows the loop never falls through.
The fix for TODO 2 is two words on the declaration: @PublishedApi internal fun giveUp(...). internal keeps it out of the Kotlin API, and @PublishedApi lets public inline bodies call it.
supplyAsync stores a thrown exception in the future, and get() reports it as an ExecutionException whose cause is your RetryExhaustedException. You don't have to write anything for that.
lab.done: All eight tests in RetryTest and RetryFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write timed and timedAsync from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an inline timed(label, block) that returns the block's result and prints the elapsed time even when the block throws. Then write timedAsync(label, executor, block) that runs timed on an executor and returns a CompletableFuture. Which parameter needs a modifier, and which one?

answer.html: inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block is called inside the Supplier: another execution context, so crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor)

alt.title: Timing.java
alt.html: static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // no modifier exists in Java: the Supplier is always an object static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); }

recap: inline copies the function body and the bodies of its lambda arguments into each caller: no Function object, no call through an interface, no boxing of a generic result.

A bare return in a lambda passed to an inline function is a non-local return and leaves the enclosing function. return@forEach leaves only the lambda. Since Kotlin 2.2, break and continue work there too.

noinline keeps one lambda as a real object you can store or pass on. crossinline lets you call a lambda from another execution context (a Runnable, a Supplier, an object) by forbidding non-local returns in it.
Inline only small functions that take lambdas. Every caller carries a copy, and a public inline body stays frozen in a caller until that caller is recompiled.
A public inline function may only use public API. Reach a helper through @PublishedApi internal.
The limit: inlining helps only a lambda that runs right there, in the caller. Java never inlines Kotlin code; it calls the compiled body and passes Function0 or Function1 objects.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the compiler made them write crossinline in inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T) = withPrinter(Callable { block() }). Explain, in your own words, what could go wrong without it and what they give up by adding it.
explain.answer: Because the function is inline, the caller's lambda is pasted into the caller, and normally a bare return in it would return from the caller. Here the lambda isn't called directly: it's called inside a Callable that the printer library runs, maybe later and maybe on another thread. By then the caller's function may already have returned, so a return from inside the Callable can't mean "return from the caller". The compiler can't allow that, so it asks for crossinline. With crossinline, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Callable class it generates for that call site, and in exchange callers may not write a bare return in the block. They can still use a labeled return like return@printing. noinline would also compile, but it keeps the lambda as a separate object, which is the fix for storing a lambda, not for calling it somewhere else.

deeper.html:
Kotlin's inlining and the JIT's inlining are different tools. Kotlin inlines at compile time, across modules, before the JVM ever sees the code. That is the only kind that can make a non-local return or a reified type work, because both change what the code means. The JIT inlines at run time, only on hot paths, and can undo its choice (deoptimization) when its assumptions break. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers that side.

The Kotlin docs say inlining pays off "especially at 'megamorphic' call-sites inside loops". The reason is in the profile the JIT keeps for each call site. An ordinary forEach taking a Function1 has one invoke call site inside it. If 30 different lambdas flow through that one call site, the JIT sees 30 receiver classes there and can't inline any of them. With an inline forEach, each caller has its own copy of the loop, with exactly one lambda body pasted in. Nothing is left for the JIT to guess.

A crossinline lambda leaves two classes behind. Run javap -p on the ModifiersDemoKt$... classes in kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/:

ModifiersDemoKt$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable {
  final kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<kotlin.Unit> $task;   // used when Java calls the compiled body
  public final void run();
}
ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable {
  public final void run();                                   // main's lambda body is pasted in here
}

The first is the template that the compiled runInBackground method uses when Java (or reflection) calls it: it holds the Function0. The second was generated for the one call site in main, with the lambda's body inside run(). Each inlined call site of a crossinline function gets a class like that, which is one more reason to keep these functions few and small.

Finally, a reified inline function has no callable form at all, because its body makes no sense without a concrete type. Kotlin still writes a method into the class file, but marks it ACC_SYNTHETIC, and javac ignores synthetic methods. That's why Java code can't call filterIsInstance<T>()-style functions.
